cells.tense: You are seeing how the whole thing fits and saying it out loud, right now, with the pen already in your hand.
cells.ask: Tell the one person it touches what you see, in plain words, this week, and stop once the sentence lands.
cells.core:
You see how the pieces of something fit — not from far off, from inside it — and you say what you see. The words carry weight because what you noticed is accurate.

The whole arrangement becomes legible to the people around you because you took the step of naming it. A structure you declare tends to hold, not because you enforced it, but because you were clear about what was already there. This works while the pattern comes to you before you speak it. When you speak ahead of what you have actually noticed — when you talk to have talked — what you built goes brittle. There's more here to feed: let what you notice land on its own before you put it into words.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a pattern to be recognized later, and declaring it now as though the future were already settled.
cells.ask: Finish one explanation in front of someone, then ask what they actually see before you add anything to it.
cells.core:
You're getting ahead of what you see. A shape assembles in your mind half-formed, and you announce it as finished — before it's been tested against what's there. You're not lying. You're braced against a future where the pattern finally holds, and declaring it early feels like getting there.

What it costs: the declarations stop landing. People hear the force behind the sentence and not the pattern in it. The structure you meant to create arrives looking like control. Go deep enough into what you're perceiving that you meet its edges — depth from genuine understanding gives you a pattern worth saying, one that doesn't need pushing. What you say then holds because the thing underneath it is whole.

cells.tense: You saw the whole pattern once and stopped saying it, and you are still standing at that closed door.
cells.ask: Build one small thing to the end this month — finish it, show it to one person, and don't call it practice.
cells.core:
The perception happens. The saying doesn't. You can tell how something fits, sometimes before anyone else in the room, and then it goes nowhere — no declaration, no structure built on it. The silence has become automatic.

What you can still tell apart is running; the outlet is what closed. To charge that, Commitment: pick one thing — a system, a document, a repair, a piece of work — and keep at it until it's finished. Sustained building is what pulls energy back into what you see. The structures that need to fall from real insight will fall once you're building something that can hold. Start with one thing small enough to finish, and finish it.

cells.tense: You are already setting up the structure everyone is standing in, and you talk about it as if it put itself there.
cells.ask: Name one structure you set up — out loud, to the people inside it — and say plainly that it was yours.
cells.core:
The arrangement around you has your shape in it. You set the terms, you framed how the work goes, you decided what counts — and you describe all of it as just how things are. You're doing the shaping. You just aren't saying so.

People feel the structure you're holding and credit the situation instead of you. That gets tiring in a way you might not have named — carrying something you won't admit you built. Gather what you've already grown: look at what's standing and take inventory. There's a quieter form of this same line waiting on the other side of saying it — structure so clear it needs no announcement. The first step is stating the plain fact of what you made.
